Kenya safari accommodation · campsite guide

Kenya campsites map: every campsite, what it costs and how to get there

Kenya has at least 202 named campsites on safari routes. They range from Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) sites in 26 parks and reserves to Masai Mara, conservancy, mountain and private campsites. We checked every one in October 2026 for its status, position, access and price. Below you'll find 187 profiles across 16 regions, with protected-area maps and a KWS fee calculator.

The quick answer

Where can you camp in Kenya, and what does it cost?

Inside most national parks, in the Masai Mara, on conservancies and at private sites near the parks. Each kind is booked and priced by a different authority.

You can camp at KWS campsites in 26 Kenyan parks and reserves, in the Masai Mara (mostly the Mara Triangle), on private and community conservancies, at Mount Kenya's trekking camps and at private campsites near the parks. A non-resident adult pays KWS USD 20 to 50 a night to camp, plus park entry of USD 25 to 90 for each 24 hours. Mara Triangle campsites cost USD 40 a night plus the reserve fee, and community conservancy sites in the north about KES 2,000.

KWS public campsites are shared and need no booking. KWS special campsites are exclusive, must be booked ahead with a non-refundable KES 10,000 weekly reservation, and have no facilities. Conservancy, Mara and private sites are booked with whoever runs them.

Why we built it this way. Before Kambu Campers existed, its founders spent about a year travelling Kenya's safari destinations in a campervan, mostly the Masai Mara, Tsavo East and Amboseli. That year taught them how transfer times, park routes and gate hours shape a day on the road. That is why every profile below starts with who runs the site, how you get in and what you pay, and only then describes the site itself. Our own base in the Mara is Kambu Mara Camp, about 9 km before Sekenani Gate on the Narok road.

    Booking and facilities

    Who runs the campsite decides how you book

    Kenya's campsites fall under five authorities and one private market. Each sets its own rules for booking, exclusivity and fees.

    Basis: KWS park pages and LN 160 of 2025; Mara Conservancy booking system; Ol Pejeta 2026 tariff; The Big North; Kenya Forest Service fees page. Read 11 Oct 2026.
    Run byProfilesBooking
    KWS public41No booking; shared; pay KWS fees online on eCitizen (KWSPay)
    KWS special34Book ahead with the warden or reservations@kws.go.ke; exclusive; no facilities
    Mount Kenya hut camps4Private hut operators inside the park; usually booked with a guide outfit
    Masai Mara reserve13Mara Triangle: online through the Mara Conservancy; Narok side: direct
    Conservancy or ranch52With the conservancy: Ol Pejeta online, NRT sites through The Big North
    Private43Direct with the owner; prices and facilities vary most

    Forest reserves are a sixth system. Gazetted forests are run by the Kenya Forest Service, which charges KES 650 per adult per night for camping, whatever your residency. Ngare Ndare Forest is managed with a trust and books through The Big North at its own rate.

    Mount Kenya's high camps are not KWS campsites. KWS lists Old Moses, Shipton's, Mackinder's and Met Station as privately run. You pay their hut or camping fee on top of KWS park entry, and you must climb with a licensed guide.

    Camping costs

    How much camping costs in Kenya, authority by authority

    At a KWS campsite you pay two KWS fees: camping per night and park entry per 24 hours. Mara, conservancy and forest campsites set their own fees, shown separately below.

    A night at a KWS public campsite costs a non-resident adult USD 20 camping plus USD 25 to 90 park entry, depending on the park's fee band. Amboseli and Lake Nakuru are dearest at USD 120 for one adult night. Kenyan citizens pay KES 200 to 500 camping plus KES 300 to 1,500 entry. Children pay less, under-fives are free, and vehicles cost KES 600 a day for under six seats.

    KWS camping fees per person per night (adult / child). Wildlife Conservation and Management (Access, Entry and Conservation) (Fees) Regulations 2025, Legal Notice 160, effective 1 October 2025; matches the KWS October 2025 tariff sheet.

    Pick a KWS campsite and your group. It adds the camping fee, park entry for each 24 hours, the special-site reservation and your vehicle, using LN 160 rates.

    Estimated KWS fees

    –

    Assumes one 24-hour park entry per night camped. KWS adds a gateway fee on some payments. Vehicle fees are charged in KES whatever your category. Hut fees on Mount Kenya and guide costs are not included. Confirm on KWSPay when you book.

    The 2025 KWS fees are still in court. On 1 to 2 October 2025 the High Court suspended the new fees on a Kenya Tourism Federation petition. KWS park pages updated in 2026 still show the LN 160 rates, and in March 2026 the Federation took the dispute to Parliament. We found no final judgment as of October 2026. Pay what KWSPay charges and keep your receipt.

    Fees set by other authorities

    Mara Conservancy

    Mara Triangle campsites

    The Conservancy's booking system lists USD 40 per non-resident adult per night (child USD 20) at both public and private sites, 2026. A 2026 secondary guide gives USD 30 for public sites. We follow the operator. Campers must hire two rangers for the night, and private sites carry a booking fee. Park tickets run 06:00 to 18:00, are cashless and are sold through KAPS.

    Narok County

    Masai Mara, east side

    Several 2026 secondary sources agree on USD 100 per non-resident adult (January to June) and USD 200 (July to December) per 12-hour ticket; children 9 to 17 pay USD 50. Kenyan citizen rates conflict between sources (KES 1,500/3,000 or KES 2,500/5,000). We read no Narok County schedule; see the Masai Mara entry fees guide.

    Ol Pejeta Conservancy, 2026 tariff

    Ol Pejeta camping

    Camping KES 3,500 per adult and KES 1,750 per child per night, plus an armed ranger at KES 5,000 per night. Conservancy entry is extra: USD 110 per non-resident adult, KES 3,500 per Kenya resident adult, KES 2,000 per citizen adult per 24 hours. Gates (Rongai and Serat) are cashless and open 07:00 to 19:00.

    The Big North (NRT conservancies)

    Northern community campsites

    Most sites charge KES 2,000 per adult and KES 1,000 per child under 12 per night. Sera and Nesesia charge non-residents KES 5,000 for commercial camping, and Westgate HQ and Lorian KES 5,000 for private camping. Rangers cost KES 1,000 to 1,500 per day. Book by email with the conservancy or tourism@nrt-kenya.org.

    Kenya Forest Service

    Forest reserve camping

    KES 650 per adult and KES 100 per child per night, the same for citizens, residents and non-residents, plus daily access of KES 200, 400 or 600 per adult by category. Ngare Ndare is reported at KES 3,000 (resident) and KES 5,000 (non-resident) with a mandatory ranger.

    Community and private sites

    Private campsites

    Published rates on this map range from about KES 500 to KES 2,500 per person per night, such as Diani Backpackers KES 600 (2026), Roberts Camp KES 800 (2024), Aberdare Cottages KES 1,000 and Mount Suswa KES 1,000 (cash only). Many rates come from trip reports, so each profile shows the year we saw it.

    Masai Mara campsites

    Eleven of the reserve's campsites sit in the Mara Triangle and are booked online through the Mara Conservancy at USD 40 per non-resident adult per night (2026). Campers must hire two rangers for the night. Olakira and Tor's are on the Narok County side; Tor's now runs as a tented camp, so check before bringing your own tent.

    Dirisha Private Campsite

    Masai Mara4WD required
    Where
    Mara Triangle (Masai Mara National Reserve). Narok County. GPS -1.33167, 34.99496. Altitude about 1,540 m (terrain model).
    Drive
    261 km, about 7 h 06 min from Nairobi CBD (routed by Mapbox; murram sections usually take longer).
    Access
    From Narok, the fastest approach to the northern Triangle is via Aitong to Oloololo Gate; from Oloololo Gate the site is on the lower road along the Mara River towards Iseiya station. Road: murram/graded park roads and dirt tracks inside the reserve.
    Cost
    USD 40 per non-resident adult per night (child USD 20); the booking system also lists KES rates for Kenyan citizens and East African residents. Seen 2026 (source). Plus the Mara Triangle conservation fee (a 12-hour ticket bought through KAPS; cashless). Campers must hire two rangers for the night.
    Book
    Online through Mara Bookings, the Mara Conservancy's campsite booking system (linked from maratriangle.org); unpaid holds released after 48 hours. Enquiries: mara@maratriangle.org Booking page

    5.0 / 54 Google Maps reviews, read 11 Oct 2026 Photos and reviews on Google Maps

    Facilities, notes and sources

    Good to know: Private campsite: Mara Conservancy requires campers to hire two rangers for night-time security (rangers are transported to and from the site). A tour-operator booking fee applies on top of camping fees (KSh 50,000 professional / KSh 15,000 non-professional as listed). Bring all gear, water and firewood (no firewood collection in the park); no bathing in the river; stay within 25 m of camp; no night drives. Max 20 campers; open January–December.

    Status evidence: Listed as available for bookings on the Mara Conservancy's booking site with a live 2026 calendar (seen Oct 2026)

    Sources: Dirisha Campsite – Mara Bookings (C); Mara Bookings – Discover Amazing Campsites (Mara Conserv (C).

    Olarro Private Campsite

    Masai Mara4WD required
    Where
    Mara Triangle (Masai Mara National Reserve). Narok County. GPS -1.47095, 35.03500. Altitude about 1,490 m (terrain model).
    Drive
    285 km, about 8 h 35 min from Nairobi CBD (routed by Mapbox; murram sections usually take longer).
    Access
    From Narok take the tarmac to Sekenani Gate, cross the main reserve to Purungat Bridge (Mara Triangle entry), then follow the main road north along the Mara River towards Iseiya station. Road: murram/graded park roads and dirt tracks inside the reserve.
    Cost
    USD 40 per non-resident adult per night (child USD 20); the booking system also lists KES rates for Kenyan citizens and East African residents. Seen 2026 (source). Plus the Mara Triangle conservation fee (a 12-hour ticket bought through KAPS; cashless). Campers must hire two rangers for the night.
    Book
    Online through Mara Bookings, the Mara Conservancy's campsite booking system (linked from maratriangle.org); unpaid holds released after 48 hours. Enquiries: mara@maratriangle.org Booking page
    Facilities, notes and sources

    Good to know: Private campsite: Mara Conservancy requires campers to hire two rangers for night-time security (rangers are transported to and from the site). A tour-operator booking fee applies on top of camping fees (KSh 50,000 professional / KSh 15,000 non-professional as listed). Bring all gear, water and firewood (no firewood collection in the park); no bathing in the river; stay within 25 m of camp; no night drives. Max 12 campers; open January–December; near Mara River crossing points.

    Status evidence: Listed as available for bookings on the Mara Conservancy's booking site with a live 2026 calendar (seen Oct 2026)

    Sources: Olarro Campsite – Mara Bookings (C); Mara Bookings – Discover Amazing Campsites (Mara Conserv (C).

    3 Region 3 of 16

    Lake Naivasha, Hell's Gate and Longonot campsites

    Hell's Gate has two public campsites that need no booking (Naiburta and Ol Dubai) and one special site, Endachata, booked through the warden or reservations@kws.go.ke. The south-shore private camps are reached on tarmac. KWS reported in July 2026 that rising water had pushed hippos into lakeshore areas, so stay in camp after dark.

    4.0 / 58 Google Maps reviews, read 11 Oct 2026 · listing: Oloongonot Public Campsite Photos and reviews on Google Maps

    A scenic site let down by uneven management and noisy weekend crowds, according to several reviewers.

    Reviewers like

    • Attractive setting in a scenic area
    • Showers and a restaurant were noted on the premises

    Reviewers flag

    • Weekend groups with loud music can spoil the peace
    • One visit found it unstaffed with toilets closed
    • Dusty with little privacy between pitches

    Summarised by Kambu Campers from 5 Google reviews, 2017–2025.

    Facilities, notes and sources

    Facilities listed: pit latrines (reported).

    Good to know: Sources conflict on facilities: one guide reports ablution blocks and showers, another says no running water or showers. Bring all water. Some guides give the distance from the gate as 2 km, but OSM places it within about 0.5 km.

    Status evidence: Listed as the in-park campsite near the main gate by 2025 park guides; OSM node present (2026).

    Sources: OpenStreetMap Nominatim: Oloongonot Public Campsite (D); Mount Longonot National Park (African Spice Safaris) (S).

    4 Region 4 of 16

    Lake Nakuru, Soysambu and Elementaita campsites

    Lake Nakuru is a premium-fee park with one public campsite (Makalia) and seven special sites. KWS warns its campsites can flood, and the risen lake has submerged the old Main Gate. Soysambu Conservancy has three campsites near Lake Elementaita, and Kikopey, Eagles Point and Kembu are private.

    14campsite pins
    14confirmed operating
    3–5 hrouted drive from Nairobi

    Numbers on the map match the profiles below. Faded pins are unconfirmed or closed.

    1

    Chui Special Campsite

    KWS special4WD recommendedExclusive use
    Where
    Lake Nakuru National Park. Nakuru County. GPS -0.39500, 36.12020. Altitude about 1,790 m (terrain model).
    Drive
    151 km, about 4 h 16 min from Nairobi CBD (routed by Mapbox; murram sections usually take longer).
    Access
    Enter from Nakuru town via the Main Gate (relocated after 2020 flooding) or Lanet Gate, or from the south via Nderit Gate, then follow the park's murram tracks. Road: murram/dirt park tracks.
    Cost
    Non-resident adult: USD 50 camping + USD 90 park entry = USD 140 per night. Kenyan citizen adult: KES 500 + KES 1,500 = KES 2,000. Add the KES 10,000 non-refundable reservation fee per week of exclusive use. Vehicle KES 600 per day (under 6 seats). Premium band, LN 160 of 2025.
    Book
    Special campsites must be reserved in advance with the park warden or KWS reservations (reservations@kws.go.ke); exclusive use. Booking page
    Facilities, notes and sources

    Facilities: none. Bring water, fuel and food.

    Seasonal: KWS warns that campsites can flood during heavy rains; since 2020 the lake has risen, submerging the old Main Gate and many internal road sections.

    Good to know: No facilities: bring drinking water, firewood or fuel and all equipment. Confirm with the warden that the site and its access track are above water before travelling.

    Status evidence: Listed by KWS among the park's special campsites (KWS park page, seen 2026); individual site condition after the 2020 lake rise not confirmed.

    Sources: KWS – Lake Nakuru National Park (campsites) (B); The Star – Touring Lake Nakuru in the wake of rising wat (D).

    Good to know: Two camping areas on either side of Makalia Falls; less used than the special sites. Water may be unreliable, so carry drinking water.

    Lake Nakuru National Park. Nakuru County. GPS -0.42983, 36.10680. Altitude about 1,770 m (terrain model).
    Drive
    153 km, about 4 h 25 min from Nairobi CBD (routed by Mapbox; murram sections usually take longer).
    Access
    Enter from Nakuru town via the Main Gate (relocated after 2020 flooding) or Lanet Gate, or from the south via Nderit Gate, then follow the park's murram tracks. Road: murram/dirt park tracks.
    Cost
    Non-resident adult: USD 50 camping + USD 90 park entry = USD 140 per night. Kenyan citizen adult: KES 500 + KES 1,500 = KES 2,000. Add the KES 10,000 non-refundable reservation fee per week of exclusive use. Vehicle KES 600 per day (under 6 seats). Premium band, LN 160 of 2025.
    Book
    Special campsites must be reserved in advance with the park warden or KWS reservations (reservations@kws.go.ke); exclusive use. Booking page
    Facilities, notes and sources

    Facilities: none. Bring water, fuel and food.

    Seasonal: KWS warns that campsites can flood during heavy rains; since 2020 the lake has risen, submerging the old Main Gate and many internal road sections.

    Good to know: No facilities: bring drinking water, firewood or fuel and all equipment. Confirm with the warden that the site and its access track are above water before travelling.

    Status evidence: Listed by KWS among the park's special campsites (KWS park page, seen 2026); individual site condition after the 2020 lake rise not confirmed.

    Sources: KWS – Lake Nakuru National Park (campsites) (B); The Star – Touring Lake Nakuru in the wake of rising wat (D).

    Mount Kenya campsites

    KWS lists Kisoi Munyao (at Naro Moru Gate), Kinondoni, Mathenge, Solo and Majors as Mount Kenya's public campsites, and camping is also reported at Sirimon Gate and Chogoria Road Head. The high camps on the trekking routes (Old Moses, Shipton's, Mackinder's, Met Station) are privately run huts that charge their own fee. KWS requires a licensed guide.

    Facilities, notes and sources

    Facilities listed: exclusive use, camp toilets, dustbins, fire-pit, water bowser (water supplied), firewood supplied.

    Seasonal: During the April–May and September–October rains the campsites are accessible only by 4WD (Ol Pejeta factsheet).

    Good to know: Murera Donga is set among acacias beside the conservancy's marsh. Booked on an exclusive basis and must be reserved in advance. An armed ranger is mandatory (KES 5,000 per ranger per night). Conservancy entry (2026: USD 110 non-resident adult, KES 3,500 EA resident, KES 2,000 EA citizen) is charged per night on top, plus vehicle entry from KES 1,000. Campers bring all equipment, food and drink and sign an indemnity on entry.

    Status evidence: Listed on Ol Pejeta's camping page and 2026-2027 campsite factsheet (2026)

    Lake Turkana campsites

    Central Island and South Island are KWS campsites reached only by boat; KWS lists South Island as a special campsite. On the shore, Eliye Springs on the west side (KES 1,500 per person, operator site) and Palm Shade at Loiyangalani on the east side take campers.

    Central Island Campsite

    KWS publicBoat access
    Where
    Central Island National Park. Turkana County. 0.8 km outside the Central Island National Park boundary. GPS 3.49590, 36.04040. Altitude about 500 m (terrain model).
    Drive
    692 km, about 16 h 03 min from Nairobi CBD (routed by Mapbox; murram sections usually take longer). The road ends about 15 km away; the last stretch is by boat.

    Drive via Kitale and Lodwar to Kalokol on the western shore (about two days from Nairobi), leave the vehicle at the KWS camp in Kalokol and hire a boat to the island. Road: tarmac to Lodwar, then murram to Kalokol; boat crossing.
    Cost
    Non-resident adult: USD 20 camping + USD 40 park entry = USD 60 per night. Kenyan citizen adult: KES 200 + KES 500 = KES 700. Vehicle KES 600 per day (under 6 seats). Special interest band, LN 160 of 2025.

    Facilities, notes and sources

    Facilities listed: water, toilet/bathroom, kitchen area.

    Seasonal: Afternoon winds can make the crossing rough.

    Good to know: Known on site as Chooro public campsite. Bring tents and camping gear. The island is a major Nile crocodile breeding site; keep away from the shoreline and crater lakes.

    Status evidence: KWS 2026 brochure and park page list Chooro public campsite as the only accommodation in the park

    Sources: Central Island National Park brochure (KWS) (B); Central Island National Park – Kenya Wildlife Service (B).

    Non-resident adult: USD 35 camping + USD 70 park entry = USD 105 per night. Kenyan citizen adult: KES 250 + KES 800 = KES 1,050. Add the KES 10,000 non-refundable reservation fee per week of exclusive use. Vehicle KES 600 per day (under 6 seats). Wilderness B band, LN 160 of 2025.
    Book
    Reserve in advance for exclusive use through the Meru park warden or KWS reservations, reservations@kws.go.ke.
    Facilities, notes and sources

    Facilities: none. Bring water, fuel and food.

    Good to know: No facilities; bring water, a fire source and all supplies. Confirm the exact site with the warden.

    Status evidence: Fisi is listed in the KWS 2026 Meru brochure

    Sources: Meru National Park brochure (KWS, 2026) (B); Meru National Park – Kenya Wildlife Service (B).

    Getting there

    Roads, vehicles and camping routes

    Most Kenyan campsites are a tarmac drive to a gate, then murram or dirt to the pitch. The vehicle you need depends on that last stretch and the season.

    Of the 187 campsites profiled, 53 can be reached without four-wheel drive in dry weather, 73 are best in a 4WD and 24 need one. 8 are reached by boat or on foot, and the rest have no reliable access report. Mapbox road distances in each profile are routed, not measured, and murram sections usually take longer than shown.

    Tarmac to the gate

    Naivasha's south shore, Hell's Gate, Nakuru, Nairobi's overland camps, Diani and the Mount Kenya gates are reached on tarmac or short murram links. A saloon or 2WD will do in dry weather.

    Murram and dirt inside parks

    Tsavo, Meru, the Mara Triangle, the Aberdares and the northern conservancies need high clearance, and usually 4WD. KWS bans off-road driving and sets a 40 km/h limit. Recovering a stuck vehicle inside a KWS park costs KES 10,500.

    Boat and foot access

    Central and South Island on Lake Turkana are reached by boat, and Mount Kenya's high camps on foot with a licensed guide. Where the nearest mapped road ends far from a pin, the profile says how far.

    Seasons and weather

    When to camp in Kenya, and when the tracks close

    Kenya has two main rainy seasons, plus a third on the coast and in the west. Rain decides whether you reach a campsite at all.

    The driest camping months are January to February and June to September (except on the coast and in the west). The long rains fall from March to May and the short rains from October to December (Kenya Meteorological Department). KWS calls April to June the low season and says most park roads may then need 4WD.

    JanDry
    FebDry
    MarLong rains
    AprLong rains
    MayLong rains
    JunCoast, west
    JulCoast, west
    AugCoast, west
    SepDry
    OctShort rains
    NovShort rains
    DecShort rains

    Blue: long rains. Teal: short rains. Light blue: third season on the coast, the western highlands and the Lake Victoria basin.

    Floods have closed campsites

    The 2023–24 El Niño rains flooded 46 of Kenya's 47 counties (IFRC). In May 2024 the Talek River swept through more than a dozen Masai Mara camps, and in March 2026 Mara and Talek floods cut bridges and access again (The Standard). Riverside pitches are the first to go.

    Short rains 2026: above average

    The Kenya Meteorological Service forecast above-average October–December 2026 rains for much of the country, with a strengthening El Niño (The Star, 26 August 2026). If you are camping this season, confirm road status with the park or operator the day before.

    Altitude means cold

    Night temperature tracks altitude. At 3,000 m on Mount Kenya frosts are possible. Lake Michaelson camp (about 3,985 m) sees -2 to 1°C at night, and Laikipia runs cooler than Tsavo. The Aberdares, Mount Elgon and Mount Kenya profiles all list their altitude.

    Wildlife and safety

    Camping safely among wild animals

    Most Kenyan campsites are unfenced. The rules that keep campers safe are written by the authorities, and several require armed rangers.

    KWS says visitors enter parks at their own risk. Stay in your vehicle except in designated areas, keep at least 20 m from wildlife, never feed animals and never leave a campfire unattended. In the Mara Triangle, on Ol Pejeta and on the northern conservancies you must hire rangers to camp.

    Ranger requirements and charges where published, read 11 Oct 2026. Sources: Mara Conservancy, Ol Pejeta 2026 tariff, The Big North, KWS tariff sheet; Ngare Ndare from a secondary guide.

In July 2026 KWS warned that rising water had pushed hippos into lakeshore and residential areas. At the Naivasha camps, stay inside fenced areas after dark and never walk to the water at night. KWS's 24-hour wildlife line is 0800 597 000.

    Rules and responsible camping

    Camping rules in Kenya's parks, and how to leave no trace

    These rules are KWS's own published guidelines, plus each operator's rules where they differ.

    • Gate hours: KWS gates open at 06:00 and close at 18:00 unless you are staying overnight. Mara Triangle tickets run 06:00 to 18:00 for 12 hours. Ol Pejeta's gates open 07:00 to 19:00.
    • Camp only at listed sites: KWS publishes named public and special campsites for each park. We found no provision for camping elsewhere inside a park, so treat the listed sites as the only options.
    • Driving: no off-road driving, 40 km/h speed limit, no hooting, and stay in the vehicle except at designated places. Night game drives are a paid special activity in selected parks only (KES 3,000 or USD 50 per person).
    • Plastic: all KWS parks are single-use-plastic-free. On Mount Kenya, disposable water bottles are banned and you must declare consumables on entry and waste on exit.
    • Fire and firewood: never leave a campfire unattended. The Mara Conservancy says firewood may not be collected in the Triangle, so bring your own. Mount Suswa sells it at KES 1,000 a night.
    • Drones: you need a Kenya Civil Aviation Authority licence and a KWS drone permit for each park and day (KES 5,000, or USD 300 for non-residents).
    • Mount Kenya: all climbers need a licensed guide. Porter loads are capped at 25 kg, and everyone signs in and out at the gate.
    • Payment: KWS fees are paid on eCitizen (KWSPay) by M-Pesa or card, and the gates take no cash. The Mara Triangle and Ol Pejeta are cashless too. Mount Suswa is cash only.

    Leave no trace, the practical version. Carry every piece of rubbish out of special campsites, which have no bins. Use existing fire rings, and keep soap and washing water well away from rivers and lakeshores. Keep to the tracks that are already there: KWS's ban on off-road driving protects the grass around campsites as much as the wildlife.

    Camping suits you if

    • You travel self-sufficient in a 4x4, rooftop-tent vehicle or campervan, or with a camping crew

    • You are happy with shared ablutions, or none at special sites

    Choose a lodge or tented camp if

    • You need hot showers and cooked meals every night. Compare options in the Kenya safari accommodation guide
    • You want one fixed base in the Mara without arranging night rangers. Kambu Mara Camp is ~9 km before Sekenani Gate
    • You need step-free access. Few campsites publish accessibility, so ask each operator

    How to book

    How to book a campsite in Kenya, step by step

    Booking runs through a different system for each operator. Match the colour of the pin to the steps below.

    1. KWS public campsites: no booking. Pay park entry, camping and vehicle fees in advance on eCitizen (KWSPay) by M-Pesa or card, and arrive before 18:00.
    2. KWS special campsites: email reservations@kws.go.ke or the park warden with your dates, then pay the KES 10,000 weekly reservation (non-refundable) plus nightly fees. KWS gives exact positions for some sites only on booking.
    3. Mara Triangle: reserve through the Mara Conservancy's booking system, where unpaid holds are released after 48 hours. Buy park tickets through KAPS and arrange two night rangers.
    4. Ol Pejeta: book through the conservancy's online booking system. Gates are cashless.
    5. NRT conservancies: email the conservancy (for example westgate@nrt-kenya.org) or tourism@nrt-kenya.org via The Big North.
    6. Mount Kenya hut camps: book through a licensed guide or trekking operator, who handles hut fees and porters.
    7. Private campsites: book direct, and ask whether the rate is per person, per tent or per vehicle. Rates here are dated because they change.

    Before you pay anywhere, confirm three things in writing: that the site is open, its exact location, and what water is there. Our profiles flag 36 campsites we could not confirm as operating in October 2026.

    • Ten northern conservancy pins shared coordinates or sat on headquarters. They are now on OpenStreetMap campsite points 5 to 19 km away (Westgate HQ, Lorian, Kisima Hamsini, Tumot, Lbaa, Lgweita, Loisaba Acacia, Mugie, Sabache, Kitich).
    • Chlobus is KWS's Kisite campsite at Shimoni headquarters, about 5 km from the old pin. Komboyo in Tsavo West moved 2 km, and Mango Tree 4 km.
    • Category changes on KWS's 2026 pages: Bongo (Aberdare), South Island (Turkana) and Ruma's Nyati are special campsites, not public. Satellite in the Chyulu Hills is a KWS public site. Shipton's, Mackinder's, Met Station and Old Moses are privately run hut camps.
    • No longer on KWS lists: Honi, Shamata public and Bill Woodley (Aberdare), Rock Hyrax (Ol Donyo Sabuk), Kenge and Professional (Tsavo West), Kanderi (Tsavo East), three Shimba Hills sites and Mpunguti. We show them as unconfirmed rather than deleting them.
    • Removed: Kisiwa, whose pin sits in a residential part of Kiambu with no campsite of that name. Not yet pinned: Ruma's Fig Tree public campsite and nine NRT sites listed by The Big North without coordinates.

    Questions

    Camping in Kenya: common questions

    Short answers; the sections above have the detail.

    Can you camp in Kenya's national parks?

    Yes. KWS runs public and special campsites in 26 parks and reserves on this map, including Hell's Gate, Lake Nakuru, Tsavo West, Meru, Mount Kenya and Mount Elgon. Public sites are shared and need no booking; special sites are exclusive and booked ahead.

    How much does camping cost in Kenya?

    At KWS sites a non-resident adult pays USD 20 to 50 a night camping plus USD 25 to 90 park entry per 24 hours; Kenyan citizens pay KES 200 to 500 plus KES 300 to 1,500. Mara Triangle sites charge USD 40, northern conservancy sites about KES 2,000, and private campsites about KES 500 to 2,500 per person.

    What is the difference between a public and a special campsite?

    A KWS public campsite is shared, needs no booking and usually has basic water and toilets. A special campsite is exclusive to your group, must be booked with the warden or KWS headquarters, carries a KES 10,000 weekly reservation fee and has no facilities.

    Do you pay park entry fees separately from camping fees?

    Yes. At KWS sites you pay a camping fee per night and a park entry fee for each 24 hours, plus a vehicle fee. Conservancies and the Masai Mara also charge entry on top of their camping fees.

    Can you camp inside the Masai Mara?

    Yes. Eleven campsites in the Mara Triangle are booked through the Mara Conservancy at USD 40 per non-resident adult per night, and campers must hire two night rangers. On the Narok County side, Olakira is listed and Tor's now runs mainly as a tented camp.

    Is wild camping legal in Kenya?

    Inside parks and reserves, camp only at the named campsites the authority publishes. We found no provision for camping elsewhere inside a KWS park. Outside protected areas, camp on private or community land only with the landowner's permission.

    Can you camp without a guide?

    At most KWS, conservancy and private campsites, yes. Mount Kenya is the exception: KWS requires every climber to go with a licensed guide. In the Mara Triangle and on several conservancies you must also hire rangers.

    Can a 2WD car reach Kenyan campsites?

    Some can. 53 of the 187 campsites profiled are reachable without four-wheel drive in dry weather, mostly private camps near towns and sites like Hell's Gate. Most park and conservancy campsites need high clearance or 4WD, especially in the rains.

    Are campsites open during the rainy season?

    Most stay open, but access can fail. KWS says most park roads may need 4WD in the April to June long rains, and floods cut Mara camps in May 2024 and March 2026. Riverside and lakeshore pitches are the first to flood.

    Are Kenya campsites safe from wild animals?

    Most campsites are unfenced, so animals pass through. Follow KWS's rules: stay in your vehicle except in designated areas, keep 20 m from wildlife, don't feed animals and stay in camp after dark. Where rangers are required, as in the Mara Triangle and on Ol Pejeta, hire them.

    How do I pay KWS camping fees?

    Online through KWSPay on eCitizen, by M-Pesa or card, before you reach the gate. KWS gates take no cash. Keep your receipt, because the 2025 fee schedule is still being challenged in court.

    Are the GPS points on this map exact?

    Most are within a few hundred metres, and 15 were corrected this month. Some KWS special sites are given out only on booking, and a few positions remain unconfirmed; each profile says which.
